content: The study evaluated three groups of children aged 5 to 17 months: those receiving sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and amodiaquine (chemoprevention-only group), those receiving the RTS,S/AS01E malaria vaccine (vaccine-only group), and those receiving both interventions (combination group). The primary study found no serious inconsistency, indirectness, or publication bias, but there was very serious imprecision due to the absence of reported events in any group, leading to a two-level downgrade in the quality of evidence. Across three countries, sentinel hospitals recorded 27,678 admissions of children aged 1–59 months from the introduction of the vaccine until April 30, 2021. Of these, 4,853 admissions were vaccine-eligible in areas where the vaccine was implemented, compared to 5,141 vaccine-eligible admissions in comparison areas. A total of 4,311 suspected meningitis cases were investigated, with lumbar punctures performed in 62% of cases and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) PCR analysis available for 52%. Among children eligible for the malaria vaccine, 51 cases of probable or confirmed meningitis were identified (27 in implementation areas and 24 in comparison areas). In non-eligible age groups, 79 cases of meningitis were reported (44 in implementation areas and 35 in comparison areas). There was no evidence that the introduction of the malaria vaccine increased hospital admissions for meningitis. In an unplanned subgroup analysis, 13 cases of possible cerebral malaria occurred in the combined 3and 4-dose RTS,S/AS01 groups compared to 7 cases in the control group during study months 0–20. From month 21 to the trial's end, there were 7 cases in the 4-dose group, 8 in the 3-dose group, and 2 in the control group. The diagnosis of cerebral malaria was challenging, and the analysis was downgraded two levels for risk of bias due to its post-hoc nature and reliance on imprecise algorithms and expert panel reviews. The study also assessed all-cause mortality. Among girls, the 4-dose group had 35 deaths (9 malaria-related) out of 1,467 participants, the 3-dose group had 32 deaths (8 malaria-related) out of 1,500 participants, and the control group had 17 deaths (4 malaria-related) out of 1,503 participants. Among boys, the 4-dose group had 26 deaths (4 malaria-related) out of 1,509 participants, the 3-dose group had 19 deaths (9 malaria-related) out of 1,472 participants, and the control group had 29 deaths (8 malaria-related) out of 1,471 participants. There was no evidence of a differential effect of the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine on all-cause mortality between girls and boys. The pilot implementation study, which used a cluster-randomized control methodology, reported 13,682 deaths among children aged 1–59 months across three countries from April 2019 to March 2021. Excluding deaths due to injury, there were 2,864 deaths among vaccine-eligible children (1,421 in implementing regions and 1,443 in comparison regions) and 4,218 deaths among non-eligible children (2,230 in implementing regions and 2,225 in comparison regions). The analysis found no evidence that the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine introduction increased the incidence of cerebral malaria or all-cause mortality. The study also evaluated the efficacy and safety of RTS,S/AS01 with or without a booster dose in infants and children in Africa. The trials were conducted in diverse transmission settings across East, West, and Southern Africa. The risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias were generally not serious. However, imprecision was noted in some analyses due to wide confidence intervals and few events. Overall, the evidence suggested no significant differences in treatment outcomes, and the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine was not associated with adverse effects on the uptake of other childhood vaccines, insecticide-treated net use, care-seeking behavior, or health worker practices.
